title: AMP eyes bank shake-up as takeover talk builds
full_text:
AMP is believed to be exploring a funding structure for its bank similar to those used by Bank of Queensland and HSBC, in a move that could put the $5.9bn financial group in play for a buyout.
The company declined to comment on the speculation, but it comes as AMP’s bank comes under increasing focus in the market.
Investment bank UBS is working for AMP.
Should AMP take a more arm’s-length approach for its banking operations, sources say this is likely to make the group a takeover target, with speculation mounting that CC Capital-owned wealth manager Insignia Financial an interested buyer.
AMP operates North, one of the country’s leading wealth platforms, which would be the main attraction for Insignia.
Market sources say AMP has been pitched to wealth management firms by investment bankers that could be interested in buying part or all of the business.
Consistent feedback is that the bank is the fly in the ointment. AMP chief financial officer Blair Vernon was promoted to chief executive in January, and his comments in May that mergers and acquisitions were off the agenda has added weight to the view that the company was being positioned for a break-up.
AMP’s bank has $17.8bn of total deposits and a $23.6bn residential mortgage book. For the six months to June, AMP’s bank generated $20m of net profit, down 33.3 per cent on the previous corresponding period.
The deal up for discussion involves selling AMP’s loans to a private equity firm that holds the assets in a wholesale warehouse facility for the bank.
The bank would still originate loans, using its brand and technology, but they would be funded by the private equity firm, freeing up capital for AMP and reducing its debt funding with the firm absorbing the credit risk.
It would generate capital-light revenue streams through servicing and origination fees.
Bank of Queensland embarked on a $3.7bn equipment finance portfolio sale to Challenger in August that effectively takes on this structure.
HSBC embarked on the same move with the sale of its $36bn Australian loan book to Blackstone in July.
DataRoom reported last month that AMP had been seeking advice from investment banks about what to do with its bank.
Previously, AMP has always indicated that it would only sell its bank if a buyer was willing to pay at least book value.
Now, some think things could be different, and AMP could be willing to offload the bank at a discount.
This is as higher interest rates and a weakening housing market are expected to take a toll on lenders.
AMP’s share price has been trading strongly, up 60 per cent in the past year, which industry experts say is due to the strength of its China life insurance business partnership. But the bank is a drag on the group’s capital, and AMP could argue that, by selling the bank – even at a discount – it could use the cash proceeds to invest in a more profitable business.
